prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

I can love both fair and brown, Her whom abundance melts, and her whom want betrays, Her who loves loneness best, and her who masks and plays, Her whom the country formed, and whom the town, Her who believes, and her who tries, Her who still weeps with spongy eyes, And her who is dry cork, and never cries; I can love her, and her, and you, and you, I can love any, so she be not true. Will no other vice content you? Will it not serve your turn to do as did your mothers? Or have you all old vices spent, and now would find out others? Or doth a fear that men are true torment you? O we are not, be not you so; Let me, and do you, twenty know. Rob me, but bind me not, and let me go. Must I, who came to travail thorough you, Grow your fixed subject, because you are true? Venus heard me sigh this song, And by love's sweetest part, variety, she swore, She heard not this till now; and that it should be so no more. She went, examined, and returned ere long, And said, Alas! some two or three Poor heretics in love there be, Which think to ’stablish dangerous constancy. But I have told them, Since you will be true, You shall be true to them who are false to you.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker claims he can love many different kinds of women, regardless of their appearance, temperament, background, or behavior.
- The speaker rejects fidelity, saying he can love any woman as long as she is not true.
- The speaker argues that women should not be faithful because men themselves are not faithful.
- The speaker values freedom and variety in love, preferring to be robbed rather than emotionally bound.
- Venus condemns the few who believe in constancy by decreeing that faithful lovers will be loyal to those who are false to them.

and by Love’s sweetest part—variety—she swore  
she had not heard this until now,  
and that it should be so no more.  
She went, examined, and returned before long,  
and said, “Alas, some two or three

outputs.L2:
I am able to love the pale and the dark alike:  
the woman softened by plenty, and the woman exposed by need;  
the one who prefers solitude, and the one who disguises herself and toys with others;  
the woman shaped by rural life, and the one made by the city;  
the believer, and the skeptic;  
the one whose tearful eyes are always wet,  
and the one as dry as cork, who never sheds a tear.  
I can love this woman, that woman, you, and you as well—  
I can love anyone, provided she is not faithful.

Is there no other fault that will satisfy you?  
Can you not simply behave as your mothers did before you?  
Have you exhausted all the old sins,  
so that you must invent new ones?  
Or are you troubled by the thought that men might be loyal?  
Oh, we are not—so do not be loyal either.  
Let me know twenty lovers, and you do the same.  
Steal from me if you must, but do not chain me; let me leave.

Must I, who came only to journey through you,  
become your permanent servant merely because you are faithful?

Venus heard me sigh out this song,  
and by love’s sweetest pleasure—variety—she swore  
that she had never heard such a thing before,  
and that it must not continue.  
She went away, investigated, and soon came back,  
saying, “Alas, there are two or three poor rebels in love  
who believe they can establish the dangerous practice of constancy.  
But I have told them this:  
since you insist on being faithful,  
you shall be faithful to those who are unfaithful to you.”
outputs.L3:
The speaker presents himself as someone capable of loving almost any kind of woman. He claims that differences in appearance, personality, social background, or behavior do not prevent him from feeling desire or affection. Whether a woman is fair or dark, kind or difficult, noble or ordinary, modest or bold, he insists that he can love her all the same. His attitude suggests an appetite for variety and a refusal to limit love to one ideal type.

At the same time, the speaker openly rejects the idea of fidelity. He says that he can love any woman provided that she is not faithful. For him, constancy is not a virtue but a restriction. A woman who is “true” would impose emotional obligations and expectations, while a woman who is inconstant allows love to remain free, changeable, and exciting. In this view, faithfulness threatens pleasure because it turns love into a bond.

The speaker also argues that women should not be expected to remain faithful, since men themselves are not faithful. He treats male inconstancy as a reason to excuse, or even encourage, the same behavior in women. If men move from one love to another, then women should not be blamed for doing likewise. His argument challenges the double standard that demands loyalty from women while allowing men greater freedom.

What the speaker values most is liberty in love. He prefers variety, movement, and independence over emotional captivity. He would rather be deceived, stolen from, or “robbed” in love than be tied down by strict devotion. To him, possessive or permanent love is more painful than betrayal, because betrayal still leaves him free, while fidelity creates a binding attachment.

Finally, the speaker imagines Venus, the goddess of love, condemning the few people who believe in constancy. According to this decree, those who insist on being faithful are punished by loving people who are false to them. In other words, constancy becomes its own punishment: the loyal lover is doomed to suffer because their devotion is given to someone who does not return it. Through this ironic conclusion, the speaker celebrates inconstancy and portrays faithful love as foolish, restrictive, and painful.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker who openly rejects the ideal of constancy in love. Instead of praising faithful attachment to one beloved, he argues that love should be varied, flexible, and free from restrictive moral expectations. Addressing women directly, he insists that he can love almost anyone—women of different appearances, temperaments, and levels of virtue—so long as they do not demand that he remain faithful to only one. This creates a witty paradox: the only kind of woman he cannot love is the woman who insists on truth and constancy.

Through this playful but sharp argument, the poem satirizes conventional ideas about romantic faithfulness. The speaker treats fidelity not as a noble virtue but as an unreasonable limitation, even a kind of foolishness. His tone is clever, provocative, and deliberately shocking, as he turns traditional love poetry upside down. Rather than promising eternal devotion, he celebrates inconstancy as natural and desirable. The poem’s direct address gives the argument a persuasive, almost conversational quality, while its paradoxes expose the tension between social ideals of love and the speaker’s self-interested desire for freedom.

The final section introduces Venus, the goddess of love, whose judgment gives the poem its most ironic conclusion. Venus decrees that those who insist on being “true” will be punished by being matched with false lovers. This judgment reverses the expected moral order: instead of rewarding fidelity, the goddess of love makes it a source of suffering. The result is a satirical vision of love in which constancy appears naïve, self-defeating, and even ridiculous. By ending with this ironic punishment, the poem suggests that those who cling too seriously to faithful attachment may be the very people most likely to be betrayed.
outputs.L5:
Her courage was quiet, but it never disappeared. And every time life became difficult, she found a reason to keep moving forward. She believed that patience, kindness, and determination could change even the hardest days.

Will was not just a name to her; it was a promise. It meant choosing hope when things felt uncertain. It meant standing up again after failure. It meant trusting that the future could still become something beautiful.

Her journey was not perfect, and it was not always easy, but it was hers. And with strong will, she continued to grow, learn, and become the person she was meant to be.

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me a metaphysical poem about rejecting constancy in love, with lines about loving “her, and her, and you, and you.”
counterfactuals.output:
I will not nail my heart to any star,  
Nor call one candle “sun” because it burns;  
The compass soul may lean, yet roams afar,  
And finds new norths at every point it turns.  

Why should love’s river swear to be a stone,  
Or flame sign contracts with the patient clay?  
What lives by motion sickens when alone;  
The fixed thing is the first to fall away.  

I loved her eye because it taught me sight,  
And her because her laughter loosened time;  
And you, whose silence made the dark seem bright,  
And you, whose name undid my careful rhyme.  

So let the moral planets rage above:  
I keep no altar, only sparks that flew—  
My truth is change, my constancy is love:  
I loved her, and her, and you, and you.
